claims.text: Refining interatomic potentials via atomistic and mesoscale simulations can reduce the sintering temperature.
Refined interatomic potentials can accurately capture interparticle diffusion and interaction mechanisms.
More accurate computational representation of interparticle mechanisms lowers the physical activation energy required for densification.
The proposed method applies to powder-based ceramic or metallic precursors conventionally processed by high-temperature sintering.
Advanced atomistic or mesoscale simulations with refined interatomic potentials can be used to re-evaluate particle interactions and diffusion barriers before sintering.
Implementing refined computational potentials modifies the physical potential-energy landscape at interparticle contacts.
The proposed intervention decreases the activation energy for surface diffusion.
The proposed intervention decreases the activation energy for lattice diffusion.
Refined potentials provide a more accurate description of atomic interactions.
Simulations using refined potentials can predict conditions that favor lower diffusion-energy barriers during sintering.
Lower diffusion-energy barriers promote particle rearrangement and densification during sintering.
The material can achieve comparable densification quality at a lower sintering temperature.
Lower-temperature sintering under the proposed approach reduces energy consumption.
The proposed approach produces minimal adverse microstructural changes.
Conventional sintering processes rely on standard interatomic potentials.
Conventional sintering requires high temperatures to overcome higher diffusion activation energies associated with standard potentials.
Powder-surface contamination may reduce the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
Failure of refined potentials to represent interactions in complex multicomponent systems may reduce the approach's effectiveness.
Simulations support a reduction in activation energy under the proposed approach.
The magnitude and cross-material consistency of any temperature reduction remain uncertain without experimental validation.
